power.title: Power Analysis Check
report:
::: {.callout-tip title="Learn More" collapse="true"}

Power analyses need to contain the following information to be interpretable: the type of power analysis, the statistical test, the software used, sample size, critical alpha criterion, power level, effect size, and an effect size metric. In addition, it is recommended to make sure the power analysis is reproducible (by sharing the code, or a screenshot, of the power analysis), and to provide good arguments for why the study was designed to detect an effect of this size.

For an a-priori power analysis, where the sample size is determined, reporting all information would look like:

> An a priori power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that for a Cohen's d = 0.5, an alpha level of 0.05, and a desired power level of 80% required at least 64 participants in each group.

For a sensitivity power analysis, this sentence would look like:

> A sensitivity power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that with 64 participants in each group, and an alpha level of 0.05, a desired power level of 80% was reached for an effect size of d = 0.5.

:::

table.expanded: All outcome measures saw a statistically significant improvement (N=69) post intervention, current energy, calmness, focus and stress (all P=0.001); Psychological distress (Core-10, P=0.001), Burnout (OLBI, P=0.023), and Wellbeing (WHO5, P=0.37) with small, large and small effect sizes respectively; maintained at follow-up.

stat_p_nonsig.report: Meta-scientific research has shown nonsignificant p values are commonly misinterpreted. It is incorrect to infer that there is 'no effect', 'no difference', or that groups are 'the same' after p > 0.05. It is possible that there is a true non-zero effect, but that the study did not detect it. Make sure your inference acknowledges that it is possible that there is a non-zero effect. It is correct to include the effect is 'not significantly' different, although this just restates that p > 0.05. Metacheck does not yet analyze automatically whether sentences which include non-significant p-values are correct, but we recommend manually checking the sentences below for possible misinterpreted non-significant p values. ```{r} #| echo: false # table data -------------------------------------- table <- structure(list(Text = "P=0.37", Sentence = "All outcome measures saw a statistically significant improvement (N=69) post intervention, current energy, calmness, focus and stress (all P=0.001); Psychological distress (Core-10, P=0.001), Burnout (OLBI, P=0.023), and Wellbeing (WHO5, P=0.37) with small, large and small effect sizes respectively; maintained at follow-up."), row.names = c(NA, -1L), class = c("tbl_df", "tbl", "data.frame")) # display table ----------------------------------- metacheck::report_table(table, c(0.1, 0.9), 10, FALSE) ``` ::: {.callout-tip title="Learn More" collapse="true"} For metascientific articles demonstrating the rate of misinterpretations of non-significant results is high, see: Aczel B, Palfi B, Szollosi A, Kovacs M, Szaszi B, Szecsi P, Zrubka M, Gronau Q, van den Bergh D, Wagenmakers E (2018). “Quantifying Support for the Null Hypothesis in Psychology: An Empirical Investigation.” Advances in Methods and Practices in Psychological Science, 1(3), 357–366. doi:10.1177/2515245918773742. Murphy S, Merz R, Reimann L, Fernández A (2025). “Nonsignificance misinterpreted as an effect’s absence in psychology: Prevalence and temporal analyses.” Royal Society Open Science, 12(3), 242167. doi:10.1098/rsos.242167. For educational material on preventing the misinterpretation of p values, see [Improving Your Statistical Inferences](https://lakens.github.io/statistical_inferences/01-pvalue.html#sec-misconception1). :::

info.title: A five-day Mindfulness Based Intervention to reduce burnout and psychological distress in UK Medical Students

text.text: Background Medical professionals face significant work overload, with excessive job demands often strongly associated with attrition and burnout.
Consequences of burnout include reduced job satisfaction, absenteeism, reduced patient care, lower patient satisfaction and increased healthcare costs.
UK Medical students are also at high risk of burnout.
Mindfulness-based interventions are effective individual-level treatments; however, more research is required to investigate the efficacy for healthcare professionals and students.
Method Four cohorts of second-year medical students at Cardiff University participated in a five-day, in-person mindfulness-based intervention.
Pre (T1) and post (T2) intervention and follow-up (T3) survey data were collected online.

All outcome measures saw a statistically significant improvement (N=69) post intervention, current energy, calmness, focus and stress (all P=0.001); Psychological distress (Core-10, P=0.001), Burnout (OLBI, P=0.023), and Wellbeing (WHO5, P=0.37) with small, large and small effect sizes respectively; maintained at follow-up.
Satisfaction ratings were consistently high, and completion rate was 100%.

Medical schools should consider implementing mindfulness-based interventions into medical curricula, as a feasible and acceptable student selected preventative tool to address burnout and incorporate student perspectives on delivery; to prevent mental ill health in medical professionals.
The global burden of mental ill health is significant, accounting for approximately 13% of the total global burden of disease.

Mental illness is now the leading cause of disability worldwide. 1 UK estimates suggest approximately 20% of the population have a common mental health disorder (CMD) with an associated financial burden of £117.9 billion in 2019. 2 Rates are significantly higher for medical professionals. 3 This includes the incidence of burnout, reported rates of which exceed 50%. 4 Burnout arises from chronic workplace stress that has not been successfully managed 5 , often classified by, energy depletion or exhaustion, cynicism and decreased professional efficacy. 6 Burnout causes severe depersonalisation and lack of belief in one's professional capability 7 , which can detrimentally impact selfesteem and ability to function.

text.text: Service evaluation of an MBI using pre, post and follow assessment.

Cardiff University School of Medicine Research Ethics Committee (REC) reviewed the study documents and proposal and considered the project to be service evaluation and under their guidelines confirmed that ethical approval was not required.

The MBI was led by Dr Manmeet Kaur and supported by trained facilitators from the Unity in Health Cymru CIC team, who assisted with practical sessions, group activities, participant support and programme logistics.

The SKY Breathing programme is a structured breathing intervention that combines guided rhythmic breathing exercises with meditation and relaxation techniques to promote mental wellbeing, resilience and stress reduction. 30 The Holistic Health Care (HHC) SKY breathing Programme was delivered in person over five consecutive days at the University Hospital of Wales.

text.text: Each session lasted approximately three hours and combined interactive teaching, experiential learning, practical skills and reflective practice.
An overview of the programme content is presented in Table 1.

text.text: Table 1: HHC SKY breathing programme -content overview Day Session Key Content Learning Activities 1 Introduction to Holistic Health Care and SKY Breathing Holistic healthcare, lifestyle medicine, physiology of breathing, introduction to SKY breathing Interactive lecture, guided breathing practices, group discussion and reflection 2 Breathing Techniques and Gentle Yoga Mind-body connection, science of yoga and SKY breathing Gentle yoga, SKY breathing practice, experiential learning, group exercises 3 Building on Yoga and Breathing Practices Consolidation of yoga and breathing techniques, relaxation, teamwork Guided practice, teambuilding activities, group reflection 4 Mindfulness and Stress Management Mindfulness, stress management, self-care, introduction to reflexology Meditation, yoga, SKY breathing home practice, stress management toolkit development 5 Integration and Reflection Consolidation of learning, wellbeing planning, patientcentred care Yoga, meditation, breathing practices, reflection, discussion and action planning 138 Participants Participants were second year medical students, aged 18 plus, currently enrolled on a five-year, taught, undergraduate medical programme at Cardiff University School of Medicine.
The MBI was offered as a Student Selected Component (SSC) within the medical curriculum.
SSCs were advertised and students self-selected their preferred programme.
Following self-selection of the MBI students were invited via email to attend a preintervention online briefing delivered by Dr Kaur.
The invitation email included the Participant Information Sheet, consent form and baseline (T1) survey.
Immediately following the final session participants were invited by email to complete the postintervention (T2) survey.
This survey replicated the baseline measures and included additional questions evaluating participant satisfaction.
A follow-up survey (T3) was emailed three months after programme completion to assess the sustainability of outcomes.
Programme fidelity was monitored throughout the intervention using daily attendance registers and programme delivery records maintained by Dr Kaur.
Anonymised data were collated and analysed independently from the delivery team.
All surveys included three validated outcome measures;
The OLBI is a validated 16-item tool measuring burnout through two sub-scales; exhaustion (feelings of tiredness or weariness) and disengagement (detachment and negative attitudes towards work).
Responses are categorised using a 4-point scale (Strongly Agree to Strongly Disagree).

Scores are presented as a total score (range of 16-64); higher scores indicate a higher level of burnout 31 and have been classified as low, moderate or severe burnout. 32 Clinical Outcomes in Routine Evaluation 10 (CORE-10)

text.text: The CORE-10 is a validated ten-item measure that explores individuals' feelings over the past week, measuring anxiety, depression, trauma, physical problems, functioning and risk to self.
Higher scores (range 0-40) indicate greater distress and are classified into six severity levels ranging from heathy to severe.
Scores above 11 indicate clinically significant distress. 33 World Health Organisation 5 Wellbeing Index (WHO-5)

Openness to using non-drug interventions in daily life and in medical practice was measured using a 5-point Likert scale.
As were current energy, stress, sustained focus, and calmness.

Post intervention (T2) participants were asked about their satisfaction with the programme, the instructors (using a four-point Likert scale), and whether they would recommend the programme to others (yes/no), with opportunity for free text comments.
Numerical data was analysed in SPSS.
Descriptive analysis calculated Mean (M) scores, standard deviation (SD), number (N) and frequencies.
Paired samples t-tests identified statistically significant differences, after ensuring data were normally distributed with equal variance.
Follow-up data were analysed using Wilcoxen signed ranks.
Effect sizes were calculated and Cohen's d interpretation applied. 36 Completion rate was calculated as a percentage.

Other literature exploring SKY breathing and mindfulness as a tool to reduce medical student burnout have shown varied results, with some finding significant reductions in burnout 23 , and others showing no change. 37, 38 This raises the question of how mindfulness interventions should be delivered to medical students to maximise benefit and tackle the multifaceted issue of burnout.

text.text: These studies speculate that minimal change in burnout may have been due to short follow-up times, a lack of available students and limited engagement and adherence.
Here the MBIs lasted eight and seven weeks respectively.

This differs to the current intervention duration, which was much shorter; which may have been more impactful due to the time constraints and high workload commitments experienced by medical students.
The observed shift from 'moderate' to 'mild' psychological distress, post intervention suggests that the programme helped to improve medical students' quality of life.
These findings share similarities with current literature, demonstrating that MBIs can support stress management in medical students [39] [40] [41] .

text.text: The practice of mindfulness encourages focus on the present moment 42 , with a non-judgemental awareness, making stress and anxiety feel more manageable. 43 Supporting a reduction in psychological distress is essential to tackle the high prevalence of anxiety and depression within medical students 12 and ensure a positive educational experience.

text.text: The current population mean wellbeing scores were above the general population threshold for poor wellbeing but, despite this, an improvement was still observed.

This is timely when studies report that medical students' feelings towards current wellbeing interventions fall short, and act as more of a tick box exercise. 49 In the report, limited engagement with interventions was attributed to time-tabling issues alongside clinical placement and inadequate advertisement.

text.text: This may create a culture within medical education, in which students are discouraged from seeking mental wellbeing support.
To combat this, mindfulness could be used to promote positive mental states within medical students.
This intervention could act as an easily accessible wellbeing service that fosters greater discussion of mental health and wellbeing within the medical community, without impacting academia.

Importantly, medical students who protect their wellbeing during their education may feel more able to provide compassionate and empathetic care, helping to improve doctor patient relationships in their future clinical practice. 50 Acceptable interventions with high adherence are critical if medical curricular is to address these pressing issues.

text.text: Free text feedback was highly positive, strengthened further by the 100% completion rate, this suggests the programme is acceptable to UK medical students when offered as a self-selected component of their medical training.

This finding is further supported by the post intervention satisfaction data; the majority of participants across all four cohorts were highly satisfied with the programme, would recommend it to others and rated the programme and instructors as 'excellent'.
Equally the majority felt that the programme had made a difference to their life, found the techniques straight forward to do, and said that they would use the techniques in future when stressed.
These findings were particularly important, as teaching people skills and techniques to cope with distress are an important aspect of mindfulness interventions.
Thus, the current service evaluation adds empirical evidence to support the effectiveness and acceptability of MBIs in a UK medical student context.
This study also sought to explore medical students' willingness to incorporate holistic practices into their own lives and into patient care.
Participants reported a clear willingness to do so which implies a growing awareness among medical students around the benefits of mindfulness, both to improve wellbeing and patient care.

In line with prior findings 51 , 88% of medical students felt there was a role for mindfulness as a tool for stress management, and 76% of students would consider referring patients for MBIs in the future.

text.text: Interestingly, findings demonstrated more positive perceptions towards the application of mindfulness in mental healthcare, rather than physical healthcare.
This suggests a need for awareness and education within medical students regarding the biological mechanisms by which mindfulness can provide benefits.
The current MBI was successful in outlining the overall benefits of mindfulness, particularly through sharing evidence of biological processes.
This may have contributed to the high satisfaction ratings and subsequent willingness to use holistic practices in participants.

Therefore, when considering the implementation of mindfulness into medical curricula, we should perhaps consider educating medical students on the physiological mechanisms of this practice, as well as the wellbeing impacts of this practice.

This willingness to use mindfulness within daily life and patient care is also seen in healthcare staff who demonstrated an in-depth understanding of the benefits of mindfulness within a medical setting, such as through accepting present situations, fostering a shared humanity between colleagues and opportunity for self-care. 52 Learning to accept present situations is essential with medical professionals, to help combat the emotional demands of their work with self-compassion. 53 Similarly, increased communication within colleagues helps to improve the quality of patient care and foster a supportive work environment. 54 A meta synthesis 52 also highlighted some of the challenges of mindfulness training for healthcare staff, which included stigma around emotional vulnerability and associated persistent shame, and balancing work and life commitments.

text.text: If mindfulness could be implemented at an early educational stage for medical students, this could help to alleviate stigma in professional training grades.
This study had some limitations.
The sample was relatively small (n=69) and predominantly female, which may limit generalisability.

However, research consistently suggests that female medical students face a higher risk of burnout 56 , driven by the unique interplay of several factors, such as heightened imposter syndrome 57 , perceived academic stress 58 and vulnerability to emotional exhaustion. 59 Nevertheless, it is important to ensure that when determining the effectiveness of interventions, that the sample is representative of the UK medical student population.

text.text: In the UK, female students reportedly make up 60% of the population and in Northern Ireland even higher at 72% and so the current sample is similar.

This female-majority trend among yearly intakes has been observed over several years and is now reflected in the wider workforce, where female doctors have reached parity with and overtaken men. 60 So, it is imperative that evidence-based interventions that support females in particular, are evaluated and reported.

text.text: Wellbeing data was not collected in cohort 1 and so this sample size is smaller than the comparison made for the other outcome measures, again impacting generalisability.
Equally, the response rate at 3 months was low (n=7) which limits the strength of any conclusions regarding longer-term impact.
This is an important shortcoming to address in future studies.

Finally, the self-selected nature of the intervention participants may have created a risk of subjectivity 61 , in which those with an interest in Mindfulness or MBIs were biased towards a potential positive outcome.

text.text: However, as mindfulness grows in popularity and becomes embedded in medical curricular this is likely to lessen the impact.

A systematic review investigating mindfulness in medical schools found fourteen medical schools across the globe that teach mindfulness to medical students, dental . students and residents. 62 Similarly, nearly 80% of medical schools in the UK offer mindfulness activities, with five universities providing access to an eight-week wellbeing course, and seven universities embedding mindfulness as a required element in the core curriculum. 63 Monash University have integrated mindfulness into their medical curricula with reduced psychological distress and improved quality of life during peak exam seasons 64 , implemented in multiple medical schools since. 63 highlighting a clear interest and willingness to use mindfulness within medical education.

text.text: The format in which mindfulness is delivered currently differs between medical schools, including simple lectures, one-day workshops and two-month programmes.
Considering this, it is also important to determine whether mindfulness should be taught as an elective or as part of the core medical curriculum.
This idea has already been discussed 62 , raising the important point that there are obstacles and opportunities throughout the entirety of medical school.

text.text: The most common way in which medical schools implement mindfulness is through a student selected process, implying that students are willing to engage.

This motivation is arguably essential for student benefit, therefore, compulsory mindfulness in medical school may not benefit all. 62 As a result, the present MBI should perhaps be introduced into Welsh medical schools as an optional component.

text.text: Adjustments should be made to offer the current MBI at additional time points, to support students throughout their whole degree.
Future qualitative research should focus on identifying student preferences for delivery of the SKY breathing HHC intervention in Welsh medical students, to maximise benefit.
Similarly, future studies should also investigate the long-term impacts on Welsh medical students, to confirm whether these positive changes can be sustained.

This suggests the programme is an effective and feasible approach to support to UK medical students' mental health during their medical education journeys.
Future research should consider the implementation of the SKY breathing HHC intervention into Welsh medical curricula, as a student selected preventative tool to tackle burnout.
It is also important to investigate student perspectives on how best to deliver the intervention and maximise impact.

Long-term studies should be completed to establish the duration of effects, and whether taking part and receiving such training can support sustained improvements in mental health, particularly as students progress and become medical professionals working within a busy and complex national health service.
